title: The forgotten formula for lovable cities - Works in Progress Magazine
gist: Works in Progress revisits Camillo Sitte's 1889 The Art of Building Cities: lovable places come from small, enclosed, asymmetrical squares with monuments at the edges and landmark buildings embedded in ordinary fabric. Modernism buried these rules, but its global repudiation and the New Urbanist revival suggest demand is rising while execution skill remains scarce.

themes.theme: Enclosure and scale of public space

insights.claim: Sitte's first principle is that the best public squares are physically enclosed and small, so people experience them as 'outdoor rooms'; the recurring design problem is that every street entrance breaks the wall of enclosure.
insights.speaker: Camillo Sitte
insights.so_what: Placemaking value comes from geometry of enclosure, not building quality, so cheap buildings can still yield high-value districts.

insights.claim: Entrance design can preserve enclosure: 'turbine squares' with one street per corner continuing the plane of the wall (Brussels Grand-Place) hide entrances from most points, and bridged or colonnaded entrances (Plaça Reial, 6 of 7 bridged) go further.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Concrete, cheap-to-specify design rules exist for new developments aiming at 'old town' feel.

insights.claim: Squares designed for carriage flow (Trafalgar Square, nine-road Place de la Concorde with buildings on one side) are weakly enclosed and feel bewildering for pedestrians; traffic-first 19th-century planning undermined public space.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Traffic-optimised plazas are low-amenity assets; pedestrianisation alone does not fix missing enclosure.

insights.claim: Sitte's sizing rule of thumb: a square's dimensions should not exceed twice the height of its principal building. Oversized squares (Madrid's Plaza de la Armería, Budapest's Heroes' Square, St Peter's Square) miniaturise the buildings and leave visitors exposed.
insights.speaker: Camillo Sitte
insights.so_what: A quantifiable test for monumental-scale urban projects; grandeur in drone footage does not equal human-scale quality.
insights.quote: the dimensions of a square should not be greater than twice the height of the principal building in it
insights.locator: Squares should not be too large

insights.claim: Fixing an over-large square by making buildings taller just swaps one failure for another: the buildings become 'meant for giants' (Les Espaces d'Abraxas near Paris).
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Density through height alone does not produce lovable places.
insights.locator: Squares should not be too large

insights.claim: The Pantheon's tiny square makes it feel grand, though it is smaller than Madrid Cathedral or St Peter's; what matters is building size relative to square, not absolute size.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Relative scale is the design variable; small plots can host dignified landmarks.

insights.claim: Symmetry is overrated: formal plans like the Place Vendôme appear neat from satellite but pedestrians never stand at the balance point, while irregular spaces like Verona's Piazza delle Erbe (a wonky pentagon) feel harmonious because irregularity is 'seen only on paper'.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Plans judged from above or on drawings mislead; evaluate design at eye level.

insights.claim: Monuments belong at the edges of squares against plain walls, not in the centre or on axis with key buildings. Centred statues block routes and views; isolated ones lose scale cues, as the 5m+ bronze David at Piazzale Michelangelo is mistaken for life-sized.
insights.speaker: Camillo Sitte
insights.so_what: Civic art placement is a cheap lever on perceived grandeur; neat axial layouts destroy value.
insights.quote: Statues should not be placed in the middle of squares

insights.claim: Sitte wanted art woven into everyday civic life rather than housed in museums, which he called 'art prisons'.
insights.speaker: Camillo Sitte

themes.theme: Buildings need context: dégagement as failed experiment

insights.claim: Great public buildings are best enmeshed in everyday housing. In Rome, of 255 churches only six are freestanding (two of them modern Protestant churches); 110 adjoin others on three sides and 41 on one.
insights.speaker: Camillo Sitte
insights.so_what: Historical evidence that the dignity-through-isolation model is a modern aberration.

insights.claim: Haussmann's demolition of the Rue Neuve Notre Dame to create the Parvis made Notre Dame look smaller and lonelier: the vernacular fabric had framed views, supplied scale and delayed full view of the facade until it towered overhead. 19th-century dégagement is a natural experiment against isolating monuments.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Clearing surroundings to showcase assets can destroy the value it was meant to reveal.

insights.claim: Sitte proposed filling Vienna's Votive Church 'monster plaza' with regular urban fabric forming three small squares; this also made the scheme denser and more spatially efficient, aligning aesthetics with land economics.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Beauty-oriented urbanism can coincide with higher-density infill rather than trade off against it.

insights.claim: Padua versus Washington DC shows a figure-ground switch: in Padua buildings mould around spaces, in Washington space is moulded around isolated monumental buildings.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Useful lens for judging whether a masterplan treats public space as primary or as leftover.

themes.theme: Rise, fall and revival of Sitte's influence

insights.claim: Sitte's 1889 book was explosively influential: within a year it prompted redrawn expansion plans in Germany and Austria, and by his death in 1903 his followers held prestigious posts in Munich, Berlin and Vienna.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: A single design treatise can reset planning orthodoxy within years.

insights.claim: Helsinki's switch from neoclassical grid to Sittesque curving streets, turbine squares and T-junctions produced characterful 'old town' effects even with the same tall apartment buildings and wide streets, showing layout rather than building form drives charm.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Evidence that street-pattern changes alone can lift neighbourhood desirability at no extra building cost.

insights.claim: Modernism amplified everything Sitte opposed: public space as leftover, parallel blocks instead of perimeter blocks, and reduced built footprint for greenery, parking and roads. Modernists dismissed Sitte as an impractical romantic.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Explains why much 20th-century development is disliked and why such stock may be at a structural disadvantage.
insights.quote: a kind of troubadour, ineffectually pitting his medieval songs against the din of modern industry

insights.claim: Modernist planning has been repudiated almost worldwide, vindicating Sitte; New Urbanist towns (Seaside, I'On, Poundbury) and practices like Ash Sakula and Peter Barber explicitly use Sittesque design, while mainstream developers follow slowly and often incompetently, producing stilted pastiche.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Demand for traditional-style, human-scale places is structurally rising; execution skill is scarce, favouring the few who can deliver it.
insights.quote: Mainstream development is moving in the same direction, but slowly and often incompetently

insights.claim: The craft of city-building was perfected over centuries and nearly lost; Sitte's recorded principles are the main route to relearning it.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Tacit urban-design knowledge is scarce; teams that master it hold a differentiated skill.
insights.quote: building cities is an art perfected over hundreds of years
